summary: A service that rents furniture and appliances to customers under plans that vary by product, city and rental period.
description: Rentomojo lets a customer use household goods without buying them outright at the start. For example, someone moving to a city for a temporary job might rent a bed and washing machine. The company arranges the items, takes them to the home, provides the support covered by the plan and collects them when the rental ends.
money: Customers pay rent and any service or other charges allowed by their agreement. The business pays to obtain or finance products, move and install them, maintain them, store them and prepare returned items for another customer. A refundable deposit remains money owed back under the terms; it is not automatically income or profit.
customers: Households, students and professionals needing furniture or appliances for a period of time. What is available and the payment, support and return terms vary by city and plan.
drivers: How long products earn paid rent, gaps between customers, payments actually collected, repairs, transport, storage and the cost of obtaining and funding the goods.

groups.title: Furniture for rent
groups.examples: Beds, sofas, wardrobes, tables, chairs and selected packages.
groups.explanation: The customer pays to use the furniture under the agreement. The company must bring it in usable condition and manage what happens when it is returned.

groups.title: Appliances for rent
groups.examples: Refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners, televisions and other available items.
groups.explanation: Appliances need suitable installation and reliable operation. Maintenance covered by the plan still costs the company money.

groups.title: Packages and rental plans
groups.examples: Furniture or appliance combinations and subscription options.
groups.explanation: A subscription is an agreement to pay regularly for continued use. Compare how long the customer commits, what is included and what it costs to end early, rather than looking only at the monthly price.

groups.title: Support and collecting items back
groups.examples: Installation, covered maintenance, relocation and returns under the plan.
groups.explanation: The job continues after the product reaches the home. When it comes back, the company may need to inspect, repair, clean and store it before finding another paying user.

basics.title: One washing machine can earn rent from more than one customer
basics.text: It earns while someone is paying to use it. A machine in storage, awaiting transport or being repaired may earn nothing during that time. Utilisation means how much of the available product time is actually being used; check whether the reported measure means paid rentals.

steps.title: Obtain an item suitable for repeated rental
steps.text: Buy or arrange the product, fund it and make it ready for a customer. Storage and funding can cost money before rent starts.

steps.title: Agree the plan and take it to the home
steps.text: Confirm the price, period, deposit, included services and return terms, then transport and install the item as needed.

steps.title: Collect rent and carry out promised support
steps.text: Send bills, receive payments and provide the maintenance or other support included in the agreement.

steps.title: Collect the item and prepare it for the next user
steps.text: Inspect its condition, make necessary repairs and seek another paying customer, or retire the item when it is no longer worth renting.

specifics.title: A large stock of products is useful only if enough earn rent
specifics.text: The company still pays for items sitting unused. Long gaps, damage or repairs can reduce what a product earns over its life. Website registrations and delivery counts are not the same as collected rent.

specifics.title: A short rental can be harder to earn back
specifics.text: Taking a product to a home, installing it and winning the customer cost money early. If the customer leaves sooner, fewer rental payments cover those costs. An early-exit charge only helps if it is due and collected.

specifics.title: Rent, deposits and product spending happen at different times
specifics.text: The company may pay for a product before receiving much rent. It may also have to return a deposit. Depreciation is the accounting charge for a product losing value over time; it need not match the date cash was spent buying it.

watch: Do products earn rent for enough of their usable life?
Idle or damaged items still cost the business money.
Look for time with paying users, time in storage or repair and expected product life. Do not treat the purchase value of all items as rental revenue.
Are customers paying and continuing their rentals?
A rent bill is not the same as money received.
Read overdue payments, unpaid amounts written off, cancellations and renewals. Where customer groups are compared, check when those customers started and how long they have been observed.
Do transport and support costs fit the plan price?
Every move, installation and repair needs people or money.
Read the costs of taking items to homes, collecting them, repairing them and storing them. Included maintenance is still a business expense.
Can the company fund products before rent pays back their cost?
Growth may need cash even while rental income increases.
Check product purchases or rental arrangements with suppliers, borrowing, repayments and cash from normal operations. Do not treat refundable deposits as spare profit.
Are the plan and the company’s investment status clear?
A rental plan and an exchange-traded share are different things to verify.

Use the current official agreement for rental length, damage, refunds and early closure. Separately check the legal company and exchange admission: an IPO document alone does not establish that shares have begun trading.
risks: Products wait too long without paying users
Wear, outdated goods or weak demand can leave items idle and reduce their lifetime earnings.
Customers stop paying or leave early
Missed rent, disputed charges and shorter rentals can leave costs unrecovered.
Repairs and moves cost more than expected
Damage, storage and repeated transport can absorb regular rental payments.
Expansion needs cash faster than rentals provide it
More items and cities require spending before enough payments have arrived.
context: Follow the item after the first customer leaves

A successful first rental is only part of the story. The item’s condition, collection and repair costs, and time taken to find another user affect what it earns overall. Regular rent is useful only after those repeated costs are considered.
quiz: Is a refundable deposit the same as profit from renting a product?
No. The agreement determines when it must be returned and what may be deducted. Rental profit must cover the product, service, collection and funding costs separately.

financialNotes.title: Verify the legal entity and financial scope first
financialNotes.text: The restated consolidated figures are verified from the issuer’s offer documents; current exchange admission remains separately unverified. The disclosed deferred-tax credit increased annual profit after tax, so the profit should not be read as rental operating performance alone. Separate recognised rental revenue, refundable deposits, depreciation, financing and cash needed for assets.
